narrative.documentConcept: Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
narrative.text: Amantadine has formulation-specific evidence for dyskinesia, while its precise therapeutic mechanism remains unknown. Extended-release Gocovri requires attention to renal function, hallucinations, edema and withdrawal. Anticholinergics such as benztropine and trihexyphenidyl have a restricted role because cognitive and peripheral adverse effects can outweigh motor benefit, especially in older people. Clinical emphasis on tremor should be distinguished from the weak trial evidence for preferential tremor efficacy. Older inconclusive amantadine reviews address different evidence from later formulation-specific trials. NICE discourages several proposed neuroprotective supplements.

narrative.documentConcept: Amantadine, anticholinergics and other adjunct drugs
narrative.text: The Parkinson Foundation describes anticholinergics as predominantly useful for tremor with little effect on other symptoms; the Cochrane review found motor benefit over placebo but conflicting results and insufficient support for a preferential effect on tremor. The latter limits claims of established symptom selectivity.

narrative.documentConcept: Dopamine agonists and apomorphine
narrative.text: Dopamine agonists offer symptomatic treatment for selected patients with Parkinson disease. Early-treatment choices require balancing motor benefit against sleepiness, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; formulation choice should reflect patient preferences and tolerability. Apomorphine has distinct intermittent subcutaneous rescue and continuous infusion uses in advanced disease. The TOLEDO randomized trial supports infusion for persistent motor fluctuations, but adverse effects and treatment withdrawal remain relevant. Product-specific supervision, contraindications, and infusion-site care are essential. The PROUD trial did not support disease modification by pramipexole.

narrative.documentConcept: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
narrative.text: Impulse control disorders in Parkinson’s disease include harmful gambling, shopping, sexual behaviour and binge eating. Dopamine dysregulation syndrome involves compulsive medication overuse; punding involves repetitive, purposeless activity. Dopamine agonists carry a major ICD risk, although other dopaminergic therapy can also be implicated. Prevention requires candid patient and family counselling and repeated behavioural review. Management generally starts with specialist-guided gradual agonist reduction, while watching motor control and withdrawal. DDS can require a different medication-reduction strategy. Specialist cognitive behavioural therapy may help persistent ICDs, but trial limitations and endpoint-dependent drug results argue against overstating treatment certainty.

narrative.documentConcept: Impulse control disorders and dopamine dysregulation
narrative.text: Naltrexone interpretation depends on the endpoint: the 2015 review describes a negative primary outcome with secondary QUIP-RS improvement, while the 2024 review summarizes failure to improve ICDs. These are different readings of the same trial, not independent efficacy replications.

narrative.documentConcept: Levodopa and carbidopa formulations and delivery
narrative.text: Levodopa supplies the dopamine precursor, while carbidopa reduces peripheral conversion and associated nausea. Delivery options include immediate- and controlled-release tablets, extended-release capsules, intestinal carbidopa-levodopa infusion, subcutaneous foscarbidopa/foslevodopa infusion, and intermittent inhaled levodopa. Extended-release oral formulations aim to sustain benefit with fewer dosing occasions, but conversion requires formulation-specific titration. Infusions can provide sustained delivery while adding tube, pump, procedure, or skin-site burdens. Inhaled levodopa addresses OFF episodes alongside existing carbidopa/levodopa treatment. RISE-PD supports IPX203 over immediate-release treatment in patients with fluctuations; it does not establish prevention of future motor complications. Product-specific labels distinguish routes, dose equivalence, and delivery limitations. Regulatory status of subcutaneous ND0612 is time-sensitive: a US complete response letter was announced on October 23, 2025, and EU marketing authorization was announced in April 2026.

narrative.documentConcept: MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
narrative.text: MAO-B inhibitors preserve dopamine activity; COMT inhibitors prolong levodopa availability; istradefylline targets adenosine A2A receptors. These classes offer distinct adjunct approaches to OFF episodes, with modest and drug-dependent benefits. Selegiline and rasagiline also have early-disease symptomatic evidence, but rasagiline disease modification is unconfirmed. Safinamide and opicapone have supportive adjunct trials, while istradefylline evidence assessments differ between the MDS review and EMA’s refusal assessment. Selection requires attention to dosing burden, hepatic function, interactions and dyskinesia. Tolcapone carries a serious liver-injury concern. Receptor selectivity does not remove psychiatric or dyskinesia risks. The claims distinguish symptom improvement from disease modification and diary-time benefit from quality-of-life improvement.

narrative.documentConcept: MAO-B, COMT inhibitors and adenosine A2A antagonists
narrative.text: The MDS review rates istradefylline likely efficacious but notes inconsistent benefit of unclear clinical relevance; EMA’s Nouryant refusal assessment found efficacy not established. These are explicitly attributed judgments from distinct assessments.

narrative.documentConcept: Motor fluctuations, wearing-off and dyskinesia management
narrative.text: Motor fluctuations divide the day into periods of useful medication benefit (ON) and returning symptoms (OFF). Wearing-off, delayed ON, sudden OFF and dose failure represent different patterns; peak-dose and diphasic dyskinesia also differ in their timing. Management requires specialist assessment and balancing symptom control against involuntary movements. Common approaches include adjusting dose intervals, reducing individual doses when appropriate, and escalating treatment when control remains inadequate. Coexisting dyskinesia and OFF may require fractionation rather than simply reducing medication. Patient goals, tolerability, disability and quality of life matter alongside time-based outcomes. The 2025 MDS evidence categories describe strength of evidence and should not be interpreted as a treatment sequence.

narrative.documentConcept: PD medication timing, interactions and hospital safety
narrative.text: Medication safety in Parkinson disease depends on preserving individualized dose times, avoiding abrupt interruption, planning administration during fasting or swallowing problems, and checking medicines that block dopamine or interact with the existing regimen. NICE and hospital safety resources emphasize appropriate timing, specialist involvement and accurate medication records. Pharmacy recommendations address reconciliation, custom order times, alerts, medicine availability and careful substitution. Protein redistribution requires nutritional safeguards. Antiemetic choice must account for drug-specific contraindications. Observational evidence about whether medication delays prolong hospital stay is conflicting, so hospital length-of-stay findings should not be presented as universal causal effects.

narrative.documentConcept: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
narrative.text: Tremor and axial disability require symptom-specific assessment. Levodopa is the principal drug approach for troublesome tremor, and apparent resistance can reflect inadequate treatment delivery. Persistent disabling tremor can warrant specialist invasive-treatment assessment. Freezing must be assessed in relation to medication state: OFF, pseudo-ON and true ON freezing need different interpretations. Reducing OFF time may help OFF freezing, but persistent gait and balance problems also require Parkinson-specific physiotherapy. Rivastigmine gait findings are promising phase 2 evidence rather than established freezing treatment. Methylphenidate evidence is inconsistent, with a negative randomized trial despite permissive consensus guidance.

narrative.documentConcept: Tremor, gait, freezing and postural instability management
narrative.text: The German guideline permits consideration of methylphenidate for freezing; the Espay randomized trial reports no gait benefit and a tendency toward worse outcomes. These positions concern different levels of evidence and do not establish uniform benefit.
